references.text: John the Baptist warns that 'every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire' ([ref:Luk 3:9|Luke 3:9]). The same motif of cutting down the unfruitful tree is found in the parable in Luke 13:7.
Also in [ref:Matt 3:10|Matthew 3:10], the image of cutting down the tree that does not bear fruit is used as a warning of judgment on those who do not show fruits of repentance.

Jesus says in the Sermon on the Mount that 'every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire' ([ref:Matt 7:19|Matthew 7:19]), the same motif as in the parable of the unfruitful fig tree.
Jesus curses the fig tree that bore no fruit ([ref:Matt 21:19|Matthew 21:19]). The fig tree as a symbol of Israel and the expectation of fruit connects directly to Luke 13:7.

Isaiah's song of the vineyard ([ref:Jes 5:1-7|Isaiah 5:1-7]) speaks of God's expectation of fruit from His people, and the judgment that follows when the vineyard bears no fruit – the same basic motif as in the parable of the fig tree.

In [ref:Jer 8:13|Jeremiah 8:13], the Lord says there are no fruits on the fig tree and that the leaves wither – a prophetic image of God's judgment on a people who bear no fruit, parallel to Luke 13:7.

Hosea uses the image of the firstfruits of the fig tree concerning Israel ([ref:Hos 9:10|Hosea 9:10]), but the people turned away. The disappointment over the lack of fruit from God's people is the same motif as in Luke 13:7.
The prophet Micah complains that he looks for fruit but finds none: 'there is no cluster to eat, no early fig that I desire' ([ref:Mi 7:1|Micah 7:1]) – the same motif of futile searching for fruit.

The entire parable of the unfruitful fig tree ([ref:Luk 13:6-9|Luke 13:6-9]) provides the full context for verse 7, where the owner's patience over three years and the gardener's intercession highlight God's longsuffering and call to repentance.

Peter writes that the Lord 'is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance' ([ref:2 Pet 3:9|2 Peter 3:9]). This explains why the owner in the parable waited three years before wanting to cut down the tree.

Paul asks whether one despises 'the riches of His kindness, forbearance and patience,' not realizing that God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance ([ref:Rom 2:4|Romans 2:4]). This is the theological parallel to the owner's patience in Luke 13:7.
